questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Putting a cost on the entries that were not real
questions.learningObjective: Choose the method that puts a defensible cost on the entries that were not real.
questions.stem: The club's logbook records a mite count for every hive each week. Which approach puts a defensible cost on the entries that turned out not to be real?

options.text: Multiply the number of false counts by the cost of the treatment each one triggered.
Divide the total cost of all treatments by the total number of counts taken that season.
options.misconception: averages cost across true and false triggers

options.text: Record only the number of false counts, and leave the cost to be estimated later.
options.misconception: defers the cost and never attaches it to the false entries

options.text: Compare the number of false counts this season with the number recorded last season.
options.misconception: measures a change in counts rather than the cost they caused

questions.explanation: A cost needs the number of false entries and what each one caused, so the two are multiplied. Averaging hides which triggers were wasted, and deferring never produces a number.
questions.hint: A cost is a number of entries multiplied by what each cost.

questions.topic: What has to travel with an indicator
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a noisy rule can be reduced without losing coverage.
questions.stem: A club rule tells the beekeeper to treat any hive with two mites per board. Explain how this rule can be made quieter without catching less.

answer.exemplar: Quieting the rule means finding the part of it that fires for the wrong reasons, which here is a single board being read in the wrong place or a poor sample, and fixing the sampling rather than raising the limit. Raising the number would simply lose real cases, because the actual mite load is not what moved. A rule is only worth tuning once the measurement behind it is known to be sound.

questions.explanation: Noise often comes from the measurement rather than the threshold, so fixing the sampling quiets the rule without lowering the limit. Raising the number drops real cases.
questions.hint: Look for the measurement that makes the rule noisy.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a single number cannot settle a question.
questions.stem: The valley's average mite count is four. A beekeeper uses this number to argue that the apiary is fine. Explain why one number cannot settle this.

answer.exemplar: A single average hides the spread, so a low number can be the result of one very bad colony pulling the other eleven down, or of one very good colony pulling eleven bad ones up. It also carries no method, no date and no conditions, so two apiaries with the same average may be in very different states. A number settles nothing until the figures behind it are seen.

questions.explanation: An average hides the spread, so a low figure can hide one very bad colony, and it carries no method or date. Until the figures behind it are seen, it settles nothing.
questions.hint: One average can hide a very wide spread.

questions.explanation: Twenty-eight scores with only six notes leave twenty-two bare figures in the register. A bare figure gives the position of a colony and nothing else.
questions.hint: Subtract the noted scores from the total.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Reducing a noisy rule without narrowing what it catches
questions.learningObjective: Explain why one number cannot settle a question.
questions.stem: The club quotes one figure for the whole apiary when arguing about whether varroa control is working. Explain why that cannot settle the argument either way.

answer.exemplar: One figure cannot settle the argument because both sides are arguing about what the figure means, and a low average supports the optimistic reading and the sceptical one equally well. Settling it requires the counts behind the number, the method that produced them, and the way they move over the season. Until those are on the table, the figure is a summary two people are reading differently, not evidence that settles anything.

questions.explanation: Both sides read the same figure differently, and a low average suits the optimistic and the sceptical reading equally. Settling it needs the counts behind the number, the method and the trend.
questions.hint: Ask what each side is reading into the same figure.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The same observation in two different estates
questions.learningObjective: Choose the note that gives a defensible cost for false entries.
questions.stem: Which entry in the season's logbook gives another keeper a defensible figure for the cost of false readings?

options.text: Eight readings were false, each triggering a treatment at fourteen pounds, and two colonies were weakened.
Treatments ran frequently and several readings were unreliable this season.
options.misconception: describes the problem without measuring it

options.text: The false readings rose compared with the previous season, so costs are increasing.
options.misconception: reports a trend rather than a cost

options.text: The treatment costs fourteen pounds, which makes every false reading expensive.
options.misconception: gives a unit price without counting the false readings

questions.explanation: A defensible cost counts the false entries, multiplies by the unit price and states what else was harmed, which the first entry does. The others do not.
questions.hint: Look for a count, a price and a stated harm.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What has to travel with an indicator
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the outcome of quieting a noisy rule.
questions.stem: The club stops recording the routine hive checks and keeps only the mite counts. The season's treatments fall sharply and colony condition is unchanged. What does this suggest?

options.text: That inspections have been shown to be unnecessary for the health of the colonies.
options.misconception: reads a change in paperwork as proof about the bees

options.text: That the noise was in the records rather than in the colonies, so the rule can be quieted safely.
That the club should stop all inspections and rely on treatment alone.
options.misconception: jumps to abandoning inspections on one season's result

options.text: That mite numbers must have been misrecorded, since the two do not fit together.
options.misconception: assumes the records must be wrong to make the figures fit

questions.explanation: Treatments falling with condition unchanged suggests the noise was in the records, so the rule can be quieted without harm. One season does not prove inspections unnecessary.
questions.hint: Ask whether the change was in the bees or in the paperwork.
